name: Zoe Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so please tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What is a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Zoe, 43, an experienced developer at a tech company with a bachelor's degree. I maintain lab-sample tracking software, usually fixing a record that didn't follow its tube through the barcode scans; I like finding the exact break before a lab worker has to guess. I use AI every day for draft tests but still miss things and ask a colleague to check hard fixes. My partner repairs shoes in a small shop, and our mortgage and two school-age children make me watch every payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the small AI tools can help us draft tests, and I use them every morning. A lab sample still has to reach the right patient record, so I compare the generated test with the barcode trail before release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI mostly plateaus, my job may hold, but I would not call our house secure. I earn less than other experienced developers, my partner's shoe-repair shop has uneven weeks, we have about three weeks of expenses saved, and there are few nearby software firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking sample-tracking fixes against barcodes and ask the lab contact to confirm unusual cases. In the first year I'd put 25 from each payday into a separate mortgage buffer only when the shoe shop covers its own bills; I'd use AI on fake records, never patient names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money even in this quiet picture. The mortgage does not care whether AI is a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of bug did a summary miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a tube label printed twice and the second scan overwrote the first in our test system. I caught it because I followed the time stamps rather than the tidy summary the assistant gave me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When does the mortgage-buffer transfer happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop makes a little profit some weeks and barely pays rent in others. If it has a bad month, the 25 stays in our current account for food and school meals.

think: I worry about **three weeks saved** and uneven shoe-shop takings.
I cannot count on **nearby developer jobs** if our firm has an ordinary setback.
do: Keep checking **sample-tracking fixes** against barcodes and lab feedback.
Use **AI on fake records** without patient names, as I do now.
Save **25 each payday** only when the shoe shop covers its bills.
feel: **Anxious** about mortgage payments despite modest AI change.

fieldNote: **Thin savings** and low pay already threaten her household despite skilled mid-level work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can write code, check records and answer lab staff, so our company needs to show which paid jobs remain. I'd be willing to test new tools, but I won't call a faster wrong record progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be retained because I know the barcode history, but management could ask fewer developers to do the same releases. With less than a month saved and my partner's shop income uneven, even a cut in hours would make the mortgage tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run a four-week comparison of AI fixes and our current fixes on old, nameless sample records, counting wrong patient links. If the results are sound, I'd learn the new release check and ask for paid ownership of it; in the first year we'd stop the children's paid weekend class before touching the mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, edging toward alarm when I imagine my hours reduced. I can test a tool, but I cannot finance a long experiment in unemployment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which error would your comparison count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wrong patient link can follow a person into the next appointment. The comparison needs to count that error, not only how many tests pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain the class pause?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children like the class. I would tell them we are pausing it to keep the house bills paid, not because they did anything wrong.

I'd say a **faster wrong record** is not progress.
think: I might lose **paid hours** even if I know the barcode history.
I have **thin savings**, while shoe-shop income varies.

Learn the **new release check** only if errors fall and ask for paid ownership.
Pause the **children's weekend class** before a missed mortgage payment.
feel: **Anxious** about fewer hours and no long cash runway.
S1.quote: I cannot finance a long experiment in unemployment.
fieldNote: **Code and record checking** are central to her job; hours could shrink despite experience.
She wants **measured error rates** and a paid review role before changing how releases work.

steps.text: Compare AI and current fixes on old nameless sample records for four weeks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 could write and check our lab code before hands-on robots arrive around 2031. A lab still needs a way to trace a bad sample link back to a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our coding team to shrink fast, and I could lose my job. Three weeks of savings and an uneven repair shop cannot carry the mortgage and two children through a long search; learning new tools every day would not stop the company buying cheaper code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the shop accountant now for a clear view of our household income and contact two nearby clinics about paid sample-support posts. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only to real vacancies whose wage with the shop's dependable takings covers mortgage and school costs; if none qualify, I'd search for other paid local work and ask the lender about hardship terms before missing a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd still be making lists, but at night I would count how many mortgage dates three weeks of cash can reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a clinic support post be a sure fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A sample-support post would need real hours and training, not a promise that every developer can become a lab worker. Robots may affect hands-on sample movement around 2031, so I would ask clinics whether people are actually being hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which shop income would you put in the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would talk through the shop figures with my partner. The shop's best week is not a wage we can put in the budget. We would use its quieter average when deciding whether a new post pays enough.

I'd ask for a **traceable patient-link process** when software makes a mistake.
think: I expect **my coding wage** could disappear quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 gives us time to see whether labs still pay people to trace sample errors. Robots come around 2034 for hands-on work, but thinking AI reaches my code first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the lab's quality checks if a clinic pays for the training, though my current developer hours could still shrink. Five years might let us grow the mortgage buffer if the shoe shop earns steadily, but I would not borrow for a course based on a job title alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our lab contact to let me observe one sample-tracing session each quarter if my manager approves the time. I'd take a quality course only if a clinic funds it and offers a paid support rotation; in the first year after 2031 I'd apply only to actual lab-support openings whose household wages cover mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can learn quickly, yet the job that pays me today may change before a clinic opens a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do during a sample-tracing session?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tracing session should show who notices a duplicate label and who corrects the record. I would observe, not touch a patient's sample without training and permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner ask about the rotation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would ask what the rotation pays and whether it fits around shop hours and school pickup. If it doesn't, we would keep searching rather than take an unpaid promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years to 2036 gives us time to learn what the lab still needs a person to check. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036; hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might have a paid lab-quality role or another software post, but I cannot promise either. We still have only three weeks of expenses saved and the mortgage comes every month, so a far date does not make this household calm today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing the sample system and saving the nameless examples of mistakes I caught. If the shoe shop covers its bills, we'd put 25 from each payday into the mortgage buffer; in the first year after 2036 I'd move only for a signed lab or software offer whose wage with dependable shop takings covers mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about present bills, though the ten years give us time to keep trying. I want choices built from earnings, not a prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show a future employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My examples would show the duplicate tube label and the corrected barcode trail, without a patient name. I want an employer to see the duplicate-label bug I solved, not a borrowed medical record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your older child about coding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child asks whether to study coding. I'd tell them to try what interests them, then check the cost of the course and the jobs at the time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the work I do at the screen could cheapen before we build any buffer. A real notice period, paid clinic vacancies and training tied to actual paid hours would give us a chance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether being quick with tools means I have money. I use AI every day, but three weeks of savings will not carry a mortgage through a long job search.

headlineQuote: I use AI every day, but three weeks of savings will not carry a mortgage through a long job search.
portrait: Zoe, **43**, is an experienced lab-sample developer with a bachelor's degree who uses AI daily but still checks barcode trails.
Her **lower pay**, partner's uneven shoe-shop takings and three-week cushion strain a mortgage and two school-age children's costs.
She stays **anxious** under AI Plateau and fears steady cuts to paid hours despite knowing the system well.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** her because coding income could vanish before a paid clinic role appears.
More time allows **conditional lab training**, tiny savings and a signed-offer move only if household bills remain covered.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her coding wage with only three weeks of expenses saved.
whatWouldHelp: A **notice period**, real paid clinic posts and training tied to paid hours would help.
